newsitem.title: CHINA: Rush to pass new HK laws whips up controversy.
newsitem.headline: Rush to pass new HK laws whips up controversy.

text.p: A week after Hong Kong became a special Chinese region, the post-colonial government has whipped up controversy by trying to get the new legislature to rubber stamp a rush of laws in its first regular sitting.

The Provisional Legislature, which was meeting on Wednesday, is at the centre of polemics over hurried laws to stem illegal immigration by children from mainland China and scrap labour laws that grant collective bargaining powers to trade unions.
A draft for new election rules announced on Tuesday also stirred up outrage as it would hamper pro-democracy groups.
The flurry prompted an interviewer at government-run radio to ask legislators if the legislature was becoming a rubber stamp parliament, like China's National People's Congress.
A member of the new China-appointed legislature, Selina Chow of the Liberal Party, defended the urgent laws presented by Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa as a necessity.
"I think there's nothing wrong with the procedure that the administration is trying to set in motion," Chow said.
The former British colony became a Chinese special region on July 1, and much attention is focused on whether it will keep its basic freedoms or suffer Chinese-style repression.

Tuesday's bid by Tung's cabinet to rush through a law to deport illegal child migrants, and to suspend labour laws passed in the last week of colonial rule, angered members of the new order as well as pro-democracy politicians and union chiefs.

Labour leader Lee Cheuk-yan, who was ousted as a legislator when China took over last week, declared a five-day hunger strike and attacked the planned suspension of the labour laws, which had beefed up union bargaining powers.
"They've targeted collective bargaining...it is a regression in labour rights, it takes away the rights of workers," he said.
International labour groups sent messages of support to the Hong Kong unions and denounced the government.

"We strongly condemn the government declaration which gives workers and trade unions legitimate cause for concern," said Bill Jordan, leader of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Trade unions.
"If this declaration is put into effect then the future of democracy (in Hong Kong) is brought into question," Jordan said.
Martin Lee, a voice of democracy and ousted legislator, said the government had begun the "Singaporisation" of Hong Kong by introducing retrospective legislation.
"They want certain results, then they work backwards to achieve it by changing the law," he said.
"The government bid to rush through a bill suspending legislation shows it has no respect for the rule of Law," said former legislator Lau Chin-shek.
Even some members of the new China-appointed legislature -- the elected colonial legislature was dissolved upon the handover -- were unhappy with the government's behaviour.
House Committee chairman Leong Che-hung said members appreciated the need for urgent action on illegal child migrants but insisted on their right to scrutinise all bills thoroughly.
"Members do feel there's really not that much urgency and it should really go through a proper channel of scrutinisation before we come to a decision," Leong said.

"We are taken aback," he said. "I hope this will not be a normal, recurrent affair...I have made it very clear...the Provisional Legislative Council will not entertain too many of these readings on one-day business."
The Hong Kong press was polarised in its reactions to the government's approach, with many editorials condemning it and pro-China papers supporting it.
Deputy Secretary for Security Alex Fong said the government could not allow the immigration discussion "to drag on", saying tardiness could lead to a new influx of illegal immigrants.
"This is the last thing we want to see," he said.
